narrative:
The model predicted an 84% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who is accepted sits around the 5.8 decile in their third year, you placed in the first decile, a substantial gap that signaled academic struggle in the later part of your studies. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your score of 20 sits far below the 37-point average of accepted students. These two weaknesses outweighed the one positive signal in your profile: your first-year class ranking, which gave a modest push in the direction of passing because it was only moderately below the typical accepted student’s sixth-decile performance.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), middle family income, gender, race, and full-time study plans played no meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your LSAT score significantly and strengthening your academic performance in any further coursework. Retaking the exam after targeted preparation and then reapplying with a stronger score would be the clearest next step. (218 words)
